title: Autumn Spring
full_review:
An old man struggles to come to terms with his mortality in the tender tragicomedy "Autumn Spring" (First Look).
Director Vladimir Michalek elicits virtuoso performances from his cast, including famed Czech actor Vlastimil Brodsky, skillfully crafting a bittersweet meditation on life's fragility and fleetingness.

Brodsky stars as Fanda, a man in the late autumn of life, haunted by an abiding fear of death. Rather than succumb to the morbid funeral fixation of his nagging but devoted wife of 44 years, Emilie (Stella Zazvorkova), Fanda, aided and abetted by his longtime friend and former theater colleague, Eda (Stanislav Zindulka), passes his days avoiding such unpleasant thoughts by losing himself in fantasies.

His septuagenarian repertoire includes posing as a retired opera maestro in the market for an opulent country estate, and pretending to be a Prague subway ticket inspector in order to cajole kisses from some pretty girls caught jumping the turnstile.

Despite Emilie's and their son Jara's (Ondrej Vetchy) entreaties to face reality, Fanda proves incorrigible. When Fanda pulls an exceptionally insensitive prank, Emilie files for divorce. But the two are reconciled. While life with him is nothing short of exasperating, Emilie admits that she truly loves Fanda, conceding that, perhaps, he is right in living each day to the fullest.

Brimming with wry humor, this minor gem is one of those rare cinematic experiences that used to be called a film for adults. Michalek's narrative swings comfortably between comedy and drama, resulting in moments that are lighthearted but not vacuous, heartfelt but not mawkishly sentimental, somber but never morose.

Brodsky's understated performance is masterful, conveying profound emotional depth through subtle facial gestures, his collapsed shoulders denoting a deep haggard sorrow. The scenes shared by Brodsky and Zazvorkova resonate with a palpable emotional honesty which eloquently captures the rhythms of marriage -- a symphony of crescendos and pauses, argument and laughter -- making many of the Hollywood depictions of marriage seem quite superficial.

Regrettably, though on one hand serving as a clarion call to embrace life, the film also promotes a toxic fatalism that extols youth while derisively viewing old age as a curse. Many of the exchanges between Fanda and Eda are elegiac paeans to lost vitality intermingled with darkly humorous, agnostic musings about the ephemeral nature of existence. At one point Eda contemplates suicide, grimly opining that it would be better if people "died young." Thankfully such existential pessimism is muted by the film's life-affirming denouement.

Tragically, Brodsky's off-screen ending was not as happy. Ailing health eventually led him to take his own life, an act that makes the issues wrestled with throughout the film all the more poignant.

Subtitles.

Due to minimal rough language, as well as emotionally complex themes, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
